subject: physics
question_text: Explain the kinetic interpretation of temperature.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 13 Short Answer Question 1 (printed p.138). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: from PV = ⅔N(½mv̄²) (kinetic theory) and PV = Nk_BT (gas equation), ½mv̄² = (3/2)k_BT — the absolute temperature is a direct measure of the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule, independent of the gas, pressure or volume.

steps.label: The two expressions for PV
lines: Kinetic theory gives, for N molecules
The ideal gas equation for the same N
steps.margin_note: Both expressions for PV must be written before comparing them.
steps.why: Both expressions give the same product PV for the same N molecules of the same gas, so they can be set equal to find what the temperature is actually measuring.
common_mistakes: Re-deriving PV = ⅔N(½mv̄²) from the wall-collision argument here. This question asks for the meaning of temperature, not the pressure derivation — quote the result and move on.
Using different symbols for N in the two expressions. It is the same N molecules in both.
steps.memory_tip: Two formulas for the same PV: one from kinetic theory, one from the gas equation.

steps.label: The comparison
lines: Comparing the two expressions for PV:
N cancels from both sides, leaving
steps.margin_note: This equality is the bridge between the two theories — it must appear.
steps.why: The N cancels because both expressions describe the same N molecules, leaving a direct relation between the average kinetic energy of one molecule and the absolute temperature.
common_mistakes: Cancelling only one of the two N terms, leaving a stray N in the final line.
Writing k_BT instead of (3/2)k_BT for the average kinetic energy.
steps.memory_tip: Equate the two PV expressions and cancel N; (3/2)k_BT is left.

steps.margin_note: State the meaning in words — the equation alone does not earn this mark.
steps.why: The equation ½mv̄² = (3/2)k_BT has T on one side and average kinetic energy on the other, with no other physical quantity linking them, so temperature at the molecular level IS the average kinetic energy.
common_mistakes: Saying temperature measures the total energy of the gas. It measures the average kinetic energy of ONE molecule.
steps.memory_tip: Temperature is not separate from kinetic energy — it IS the average kinetic energy, scaled by k_B.

steps.label: Independent of the gas
steps.mark_note: No dependence on gas, P or V

steps.margin_note: Name at least one thing the result does NOT depend on — gas, pressure or volume.
steps.why: ½mv̄² = (3/2)k_BT contains no term for which gas it is, or for P or V, so the result holds for every ideal gas at a given temperature.
common_mistakes: Saying heavier molecules have more kinetic energy at the same temperature. Their average kinetic energy is the same; only their speed is smaller.
steps.memory_tip: Same temperature, same average kinetic energy, whatever the gas.

insider_note: This is an explain question about the MEANING of the result, not a derivation — quoting PV = ⅔N(½mv̄²) as a known result and moving to the comparison saves time the derivation would cost.
